abstract: Mary Beech, a visiting fellow at the Washington Center for Equitable Growth and formerly director of workers and technology policy at the US Department of Labor, maps the entire federal labor-data infrastructure against a single question: can it tell us whether AI is changing the US labor market? Her answer is no. The brief is the first of three; the next two will make recommendations. Rather than argue that data are missing, Beech shows that the data largely exist but are fragmented, lagged, inconsistently defined, and, crucially, unlinked. The sharpest instance is internal to one agency: Census collects firm-level AI adoption through BTOS and the Annual Business Survey and separately holds worker-level employment and earnings through LEHD, and the two are not connected. She walks four questions in turn - who is unemployed, what is happening to wages, what jobs exist, and which firms have adopted AI - and catalogs the specific limitation of each source against each question. The brief is directly relevant to jobsdata.ai because it is an authoritative statement of why the site's own measurement disclaimers are necessary, and because it is written by someone who ran this policy area inside DOL.
keyFindings: Headline judgment: 'Existing federal data sources cannot be used yet to conclusively show whether and how AI might be driving changes in the U.S. labor market.'

The binding constraint is linkage rather than collection: 'The Business Trends and Outlook Survey and Annual Business Survey adoption data are not linked to the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics data, wage records, or other worker-level outcomes, even though both datasets sit within the Census Bureau.' NLx job postings are likewise unlinked to BTOS or ABS, so a firm's self-reported AI use cannot be tied to its hiring.

On BTOS specifically, the series that anchors the jobsdata.ai adoption chart: it 'asks firms a yes or no question about whether they have adopted AI and whether they plan to in the next year. Because this is a binary measure, it does not capture how or to what extent firms use AI.' The Annual Business Survey asks richer questions but they are 'inconsistent across cycles,' and the 2023 cycle 'did not distinguish between different types of AI or automation.'

Unemployment measurement gaps: CPS response rates have declined over the past decade and the survey cannot resolve individual occupations such as computer programmers; UI claims exclude independent contractors, the previously unemployed and benefit-exhaustees, and BLS estimates that in some years most unemployed people did not apply for UI at all; WARN notices go to states, not the federal government, and exclude remote workers, smaller employers and contractors; LEHD carries a 4-6 month lag and has industry but no occupation codes.

Wage measurement gaps: 'Most sources lack hours worked, making it impossible to distinguish changes in earnings from wage rate cuts or reduced hours.' CES has payroll precision but no demographics or occupation; ACS asks for income over the previous 12 months so cannot see within-year moves; OEWS surveys employers and misses independent contractors; IRS data include 1099 income but arrive a year or more late.

Job-availability gaps: JOLTS samples roughly 16,000 establishments with no occupational detail; NLx covers only online postings and misses referral, internal-promotion and word-of-mouth hires; private postings datasets use proprietary unverifiable methods and are contaminated by ghost postings, which 'accounted for between 18 percent and 22 percent of online job listings in one 2024 analysis.'

O*NET, the substrate for most AI exposure measures, 'encompasses more than 900 occupation profiles' but each is 'updated infrequently, with an average sample of only 71 observations; the dataset is not designed for longitudinal research; and some data collection occurred as far back as 2006.'

A broader definition of adoption gives a far higher number: a 2024 OECD survey of more than 6,000 firms across six countries including the US found algorithmic management tools - software that partially or fully automates managerial functions such as instructing, monitoring and evaluating workers - 'are already widespread among U.S. firms, with 90 percent of those responding to the survey having adopted at least one such tool.'

Institutional response underway: the Department of Labor has announced an AI Workforce Research Hub with BLS, Census and BEA to produce recurring analysis of AI adoption, displacement and wage effects; the bipartisan Workforce Transparency Act and AI Workforce PREPARE Act would impose new federal data-collection requirements; the Workforce Information Advisory Council has called for infrastructure improvements.
methodology: Descriptive policy issue brief. No original data collection or empirical estimation. Beech inventories federal and quasi-federal data sources - CPS, UI claims, LEHD, WARN, CES, National Compensation Survey, National Longitudinal Surveys, ACS, OEWS, IRS filings, NLx, JOLTS, H-1B disclosures, BLS Employment Projections, registered apprenticeship reporting, BTOS, Annual Business Survey and O*NET - and evaluates each against four questions: who is unemployed, what is happening to wages and earnings, what jobs and opportunities exist, and which firms have adopted AI. Quantitative claims are sourced to third parties (BLS, OECD, a Wall Street Journal report on ghost postings, an arXiv critique of O*NET). Four figures diagram the source landscape for each question.
qualifiers: Tier 2: think-tank policy brief, not peer-reviewed research, from an organization with an explicit distributional and pro-worker analytic frame. It contains no labor-market measurement of its own, so nothing here is plottable - its contribution is a caveat on the instruments behind the plotted series, which is why it enters jobsdata.ai as overlays rather than data points. The OECD 90 percent algorithmic-management figure is the one number that could be mistaken for an adoption estimate: it covers a different construct than BTOS (managerial-function automation rather than AI use in business functions), draws on a self-selected sample of survey responders across six countries, and predates the 2024 survey field date, so it is not comparable to the 21.8% BTOS reading. Beech previously served in the Biden administration at DOL and OSTP, which gives her unusual visibility into the agency constraints described and also situates the brief within a particular policy tradition. This is brief one of three; the recommendations that would make it actionable have not been published yet, so it is worth watching for parts two and three.
